tldr: A quadruped parkour approach that reconstructs clean depth from noisy depth and aligns latent representations via contrastive learning during simulation training, completely eliminating the need for manual post-processing filter tuning at real-world deployment.
hero_caption: Overview of DAWN's training and real-world deployment pipeline. Two training-only losses shown in green (a denoising reconstruction loss targeting clean depth and a contrastive loss aligning the latent space) enable noise-robust action decisions at inference time without post-processing filters or additional computational cost.
overview:
Research on vision-based quadrupedal parkour—traversing stairs, steps, and jumping over gaps using camera depth information—has advanced rapidly in recent years. However, an implicit assumption has remained: training in simulation assumes clean, noise-free depth, while deployment to real hardware relies on carefully hand-tuning the sensor's post-processing filters to suppress noise. These filters have dozens of interdependent parameters, their values are rarely disclosed in papers, and they require recalibration whenever lighting or ground material changes.

The authors asked: instead of filtering noise before feeding it to the model, why not have the world model (the internal model predicting environment transitions) learn noise-invariant representations itself? Their proposed framework, DAWN, builds on the Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM) and adds two simple modifications during training. First, "denoising reconstruction," where noisy depth is fed to the encoder while clean depth serves as the reconstruction target. Second, "contrastive learning," which pulls latent representations of noisy and clean depth closer together.

In simulation experiments covering stairs, gaps, and steps, DAWN achieved an average success rate of 96.9%, closing 77% of the performance gap to an ideal oracle provided with clean depth. Furthermore, in zero-shot transfer (deployment without fine-tuning) on a physical Unitree Go1 fed raw depth directly without any manual filter calibration, the robot successfully traversed stairs up to 18 cm, cleared gaps up to 70 cm, and mounted steps up to 45 cm.
contributions: Proposal of DAWN, a framework that integrates depth denoising and representation alignment directly into world model training, eliminating tedious manual filter tuning at real-world deployment.
A training-only architectural design that incurs zero additional inference cost and avoids overfitting to any specific noise distribution.
Demonstration of zero-shot parkour on a physical Unitree Go1 across indoor and outdoor stairs, steps, and gaps using only raw depth observations with all internal filters disabled.
Ablation studies revealing that reconstruction-level denoising and latent-level contrastive alignment complement each other to produce additive performance gains in representation learning.

sections.heading: Why Has Depth Noise Been Overlooked in Parkour Research?
sections.summary: While vision-based quadrupedal parkour has achieved impressive results, most systems rely on hand-tuned post-processing filters at deployment, hindering reproducibility. DAWN resolves this reliance at its root by making the world model's internal representation inherently robust to noise.
sections.details:
Advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have enabled quadrupedal robots to traverse rough terrain with agility. While proprioceptive inputs like joint angles suffice for gentle slopes and modest stairs, forward-facing depth cameras become indispensable for gaps and tall steps where terrain geometry must be perceived before touchdown.

However, most prior studies assume clean, noise-free depth images during simulation training and rely on manual post-processing filters in drivers like Intel RealSense at deployment. RealSense filter suites involve 12 to 24 interdependent parameters, with optimal values shifting depending on ambient lighting, obstacle material, and distance. These settings are rarely reported in papers, significantly hindering reproducibility.

Existing countermeasures include domain randomization, heuristic data augmentations, and standalone denoising modules. Yet these remain input-level fixes that either have limited expressive capacity or require extra onboard hardware.

Here is the key idea: DAWN embeds noise robustness directly into the world model (RSSM) used for policy learning. By feeding noisy depth to the encoder while having the decoder reconstruct clean depth—creating an "input-target mismatch"—and coupling this with contrastive learning to align latent representations, the model learns to discard noise. Because both mechanisms are applied solely during training, runtime inference cost on real robots remains identical to standard world model-based methods.

sections.heading: At the Crossroads of Visual Locomotion, Sim-to-Real, World Models, and Contrastive Learning
sections.summary: We review four research lines: visual parkour, depth Sim-to-Real transfer, world model-based locomotion, and contrastive learning. DAWN unifies these to pioneer a representation learning approach for spatial depth noise.
sections.details:
### Vision-Based Legged Locomotion
Privileged learning (training a teacher with simulator ground truth and distilling into a student) has been the dominant paradigm. Recently, methods like WMP (World Model-based Perception) use RSSM to train perception and policy end-to-end, achieving high parkour agility. However, both still rely on hand-tuned filters in real-world deployment.

### Depth Sim-to-Real Transfer
Real stereo depth cameras suffer from edge dropout where disparity matching fails at object boundaries, as well as distinct noise from sunlight and infrared interference. While noise simulation and data augmentation have been studied to mimic these effects, they remain input-level strategies; none have replaced the world model's reconstruction objective to eliminate filter dependency.

### World Models for Legged Robots
In world model-based locomotion, prior work has filtered low-dimensional, roughly i.i.d. proprioceptive noise. However, world models had not yet been applied to process depth noise with complex spatial structure, which concentrates along geometric edges and grows nonlinearly with distance.

### Contrastive Representation Learning in Locomotion
Contrastive learning (such as SimCLR), widely used in representation learning, has been adopted in robotics for teacher-student distillation and feature generalization. DAWN introduces this as a regularizer in world models to align latent features of noisy observations with their clean counterparts.

sections.heading: Reforging the World Model: Denoising Reconstruction and Contrastive Alignment
sections.summary: Keeping the underlying RSSM architecture unchanged, DAWN modifies only two training signals: a loss reconstructing clean depth from noisy depth, and a contrastive loss pulling their latent representations together.
sections.details:
### World Model Preliminaries (WMP)
Let the observation at step $t$ be $x_t = (d_t, o^\text{p}_t)$, where $d_t$ is the depth image and $o^\text{p}_t$ is proprioception. The RSSM maintains a deterministic state $h_t$ via a GRU-based sequence model and computes a stochastic state $z_t$ through an observation encoder, simultaneously generating a prior prediction $\hat{z}_t$ and an observation reconstruction $\hat{x}_t$. The policy takes $h_t$ to select actions. In standard WMP, both the encoder input and the decoder target are the identical clean observation $x^\text{c}_t$.

### Denoising Reconstruction Objective
In DAWN, the encoder receives a noisy depth observation $x^\text{n}_t = (d^\text{n}_t, o^\text{p}_t)$ passed through a noise model, while the decoder's reconstruction target remains clean depth $x^\text{c}_t$.
This works through the information bottleneck principle. The RSSM's KL regularization term constrains the informational capacity of the latent state $z^\text{n}_t$. Because the noise component $\epsilon$ in the input provides no utility for reconstructing clean depth, the model is compelled to discard noise and preserve only the information necessary for terrain geometry in the latent state.

### Contrastive Latent Alignment
Reconstruction alone does not guarantee a well-structured latent space geometry. Therefore, the latent state from the clean image $z^\text{c}_t$ and that from the noisy image $z^\text{n}_t$ in the same scene are mapped into an embedding space via an MLP projection head $g_\psi$, where the NT-Xent loss (a cosine similarity-based contrastive loss used in SimCLR) is applied. Pairs from the same environment are pulled together, while pairs from different environments in the batch are pushed apart. Routing through the projection head prevents representation collapse, ensuring task-relevant policy information is not excessively stripped away.

At deployment, the projection head is discarded and the decoder is unused. Raw noisy depth is fed directly into the encoder, and $h_t$ drives the policy, keeping runtime computational complexity exactly identical to the baseline.

captions.F1: Architecture of DAWN during training and real-world deployment. During training (left), the denoising reconstruction loss (bottom green) uses noisy images at the encoder and clean images at the decoder, while a contrastive loss (top green) is applied via an MLP projection head. On the physical robot (right), auxiliary modules are removed, and a robust latent state is formed directly from raw depth to drive the policy.

sections.heading: From Simulation Benchmarks to Demanding Outdoor Real-Robot Tests
sections.summary: DAWN achieved a 96.9% success rate across diverse obstacles in simulation, substantially outperforming baselines. On a physical Unitree Go1, it traversed stairs, steps, and gaps indoors and outdoors using raw depth without any filtering.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Noise Model
Simulations were conducted in IsaacLab (4,096 parallel environments) with a Unitree Go1 quadruped at a 50 Hz control frequency and a 10 Hz depth update rate ($64\times 64$ pixels). To mirror noise from an onboard RealSense D435i, the noise model combines Gaussian noise, geometric gradient-based edge dropout (up to 60% probability), and distant infrared interference particle noise.

### Baseline Comparisons (Simulation)
Across three terrain types—Stairs (6–18 cm), Gaps (10–90 cm), and Steps (10–54 cm)—DAWN achieved an average success rate of 96.9%. This closes 77% of the performance gap between the clean-depth Oracle and standard WMP. It also decisively outperformed "WMP w/ N," which merely saw noisy images during training, proving that structuring the latent representations is essential.

### Ablations and Noise Intensity Sweeps
Component contributions were evaluated on the most difficult Level 5 environments. Compared to noise-only training (WMP w/ N), adding denoising reconstruction alone improved success by +5.7%, and adding contrastive alignment alone improved it by +4.6%. Combining both in DAWN yielded +11.5% (an 88.2% success rate), showing an additive synergy.
In noise intensity sweep experiments scaling noise from training levels ($\times 1.0$) up to an unseen $\times 2.0$, baseline performance degraded sharply, while DAWN's drop was limited to just 6.5%.

### Real-World Experiments (Zero-Shot Parkour on Go1)
Evaluations on the physical robot were conducted with all onboard post-processing filters turned off. While all methods performed reasonably well indoors, decisive differences emerged outdoors, where sunlight-induced IR interference and surface reflectance drastically elevate depth noise. On 18 cm stairs, DAWN achieved 80% (vs. 70% for WMP w/ N, 60% for WMP); on 70 cm gaps, DAWN achieved 60% (vs. 40%, 30%); and on 45 cm steps, DAWN achieved 70% (vs. 50%, 50%), demonstrating compelling robustness in challenging environments without any manual tuning.

Noisy observations (open circles) and clean observations (filled circles) overlap tightly within each terrain class, visually confirming that noise components are filtered from the latent space while terrain geometry is preserved.

sections.heading: From Hand-Crafted Filter Tuning to Learned Robust Representations
sections.summary: By modifying only the world model's reconstruction target and introducing contrastive learning during training, DAWN achieves strong depth-noise robustness without increasing inference overhead. This marks a major step toward practical visual locomotion free from manual filter calibration.
sections.details:
DAWN eliminates the long-standing operational bottleneck in quadrupedal visual parkour: relying on hand-tuned filters to manage real-world depth noise.

Without altering the core architecture, combining the information bottleneck principle ("reconstructing clean images from noisy inputs") with contrastive learning ("building noise-invariant feature representations") enables the world model to extract geometrically essential terrain information. As a result, the robot negotiates stairs and gaps directly from raw depth images without adding a single millisecond to real-time inference.

As future work, the authors note that while their noise simulation was calibrated to the RealSense D435i, extending the framework to sensors with different operating principles, such as other stereo cameras or Time-of-Flight (ToF) sensors, remains an exciting direction to explore.

takeaways: The input-target mismatch design—feeding noisy inputs while reconstructing ground-truth clean targets—is an effective mechanism for purging noise from encoders via the information bottleneck principle.
Pairing denoising reconstruction with contrastive learning (SimCLR) structures the latent space geometry, generating additive performance gains beyond using either technique in isolation.
Applying regularizers to components discarded at test time (the decoder and projection head) is an ideal design pattern for onboard robotics where computational budgets are strictly constrained.

Because outdoor environments degrade depth quality heavily via sunlight and IR interference, learning noise-invariant representations during simulation training is decisive for real-world Sim-to-Real success.
limitations: Because the simulation noise model is designed around the physical characteristics of the RealSense D435i, whether it generalizes out-of-the-box to depth sensors with fundamentally different principles (e.g., LiDAR or monocular ToF) remains unverified.
In scenes with extreme noise where terrain edges are almost entirely wiped out, the world model may fail to recover adequate geometric structure from prior dynamics alone.

The framework requires perfectly clean ground-truth depth from a simulator as the reconstruction target, making it non-trivial to apply directly to fully offline RL setups that rely exclusively on real-world logs.
